name: Freya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; this is confidential, and your name won't go in our findings. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 43, a junior lineworker. I open the crew tablet at the depot, check the insulated bucket and spare connectors, then ride out to the job with a lead who checks my setup. I use an AI assistant every day to find a manual page or turn equipment notes into a short checklist.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which part gives you satisfaction, and which part takes the most out of you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like learning to work at height without making the rest of the crew wait for me. The concentration is tiring, and at home my partner and I have two children, ages 5 and 16, and a mortgage to cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I can let the app sort the connector box, but I still count the insulation rating twice. It saves a few minutes of searching without changing the care we take beside a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think a small routine change takes my field job. My pay is modest and our savings are less than one month's costs, so the mortgage still leaves us watching each bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the approved assistant for manual lookup and learn which pages it points me to most accurately. I would keep my current shifts and ask my lead to check my connector inventory before each job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm calm about my work in this picture, but anxious about our thin buffer. A routine tool doesn't make the mortgage or school costs any lighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still inspect yourself even if the assistant gave a confident answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd read the rating stamped on the connector and compare it with the work order. A tidy checklist doesn't tell me whether a part has a crack or was left in rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your partner and you handle an unexpected household bill now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We first delay a non-urgent purchase and check whether the appliance can be repaired. We don't use the children's school money to cover a bill unless there is no other choice.

think: I don't expect the plateau to take my **field job**.
I worry about **fixed bills** because our savings cover less than a month.
do: Keep using the approved assistant for **manual lookup**.
Ask the lead to check my **connector inventory** before jobs.
feel: I'm calm about work but **anxious** about our thin household buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a complete digital order doesn't make the wire in the bucket less physical. It may save the planner time, but the crew still needs a lead to decide who handles each part of the lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry the company will expect fewer planners and put more last-minute changes onto junior crews. If that cuts my hours, there are not many other line teams near our home to take me on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant every day and show the lead where a manual summary needs correction. I would ask the utility for a paid bucket-rescue practice session and track any change to my field hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about fewer paid hours, even if the technology is interesting. I need to know how it changes the roster rather than assume that new software creates a new job for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of mistake would make you stop trusting a summary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it lists a connector that doesn't match the work order, I'd stop using that summary until the lead checks the source manual. A confident sentence is no use if the part is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the lead to track alongside your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lead to note how many field jobs I complete under supervision and which tasks I can now do safely. That record could help me show another utility what I've actually learned.

think: I worry that **fewer planners** could mean more changes for junior crews.
I have few nearby teams to replace **lost hours**.
do: Keep using the assistant and correct **manual summaries** with the lead.
Request paid **bucket-rescue practice** and track field hours.
feel: I'm **anxious** about wages, though curious about useful technology.
S1.quote: I'd say a complete digital order doesn't make the wire in the bucket less physical.

steps.text: Continue using the assistant and verify manual summaries with the lead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the crew needs a clear notice period before the company changes our work or removes shifts. The field jobs may continue until robots arrive around 2031, but the thinking work changes immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have a few years to keep working outside, but I can't assume the utility keeps my junior position until 2031. My partner and I have little savings, and a sudden drop in my pay would reach the mortgage fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the worker representative for paid training and a notice rule before any crew cuts. In 2028 I wouldn't switch to planning or records as a safe career, because AGI can do that thinking work. In 2029, if I'm still on shift, I'd take an employer-paid high-voltage rescue course and keep earning while field work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about income more than the machines themselves. Two years is too short for me to save much, but paid training could give me a useful skill before robots reach the field work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the children's costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that we should keep the younger child's school schedule steady and postpone buying a newer car. I don't want to promise more activities and then cancel them if my hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that rescue course worth the time away from your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want an instructor to supervise the practical drills and the utility to pay for the hours. I would not take unpaid leave or borrow money for a course with no clear field use.

I say the field may continue, but **thinking work changes first**.
think: I may have field work until **2031**, but my junior role is not guaranteed.
I won't move to **planning or records** as a safe job after AGI.
do: Ask the worker representative for **paid training** and notice before cuts.

feel: I'm **anxious** about income, though paid training would give me a next step.
S2.quote: I'd say the crew needs a clear notice period before the company changes our work or removes shifts.
fieldNote: She asks for paid practice because a **certificate alone** would not prepare her.
Her household would avoid a major **car purchase** while her hours are uncertain.
She does not treat planning work as protection after **thinking AGI**.

steps.text: Ask the worker representative to secure notice before crew cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives me time to get more practical sign-offs and watch how the utility handles field crews. The desk work would change in 2031, and the robot date is three years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when AGI arrives and 51 when robots arrive. I would have time to improve as a lineworker, but I still might be on the first list if the utility reduces junior shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for paid supervision on bucket rescue and keep each task signed off. In 2032, the first year after AGI, I'd stay on field shifts while they last, take a funded repair qualification, and apply to a nearby utility only if my current roster shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but five years lets me build a practical record before the thinking work changes. I would still need to check what jobs are actually open before moving my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you apply rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the utility removed my regular field days or stopped funding the course, I'd submit an application to the neighboring service company. I'd compare its wages and shift times with what we have before accepting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the paid qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a supervisor to watch the drills and record the actual field tasks I can do. I don't expect a new qualification to make the work permanently safe from robots.

I want to know how the utility plans for the **2034 robots**.

S3.quote: I'd say five years gives me time to get more practical sign-offs and watch how the utility handles field crews.
fieldNote: She wants supervised drills recorded as **actual field skills**.

steps.text: Keep current field shifts while the utility offers them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets people plan around actual dates, but the utility should show field staffing and training plans before the last year. No one can promise the current crew work stays after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when the robots do. I have time to build experience, but I won't count on records or control-room work once AGI can do thinking tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep a record of the practical sign-offs and ask the utility for paid course dates. In 2037, if field jobs remain, I'd compare my wages, take employer-paid hands-on training if available, and avoid moving the family until I know the younger child's next school plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ten years give me more choices, but I still have less than a month's costs saved now. I'm anxious about today's mortgage and school bills as well as the later robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the younger child's school plans mean for a possible move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2037 my youngest will be 16 and our older child will be 27. My partner and I would wait until we know the school or training plan before moving to chase a field job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you decide whether to stay with the utility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the actual crew roster, pay for any practical role, and a date for paid training. I can compare those facts with my household needs, but an open vacancy doesn't guarantee the same work lasts through 2039.

I won't promise that today's crew work remains after **2039**.
think: I'll be **53** at AGI and **56** when robots arrive.
I won't count on **records or control-room work** after AGI.
do: Keep a record of **practical sign-offs** and request course dates now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots may arrive around 2031 before I have much saved. Paid field training and a clear roster plan would help me prepare without pretending that a later job is guaranteed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A course calendar turns a decade from a warning into a date I can plan around. I'd want the company to say who pays for the course and which field tasks I can practise before the roster changes.

headlineQuote: A course calendar turns a decade from a warning into a date I can plan around.
portrait: Freya is a **43-year-old junior** lineworker with a partner, two children and a mortgage.
She uses an AI assistant daily for **manual lookup**, while checking field safety herself.
Her **thin savings** make any loss of paid hours difficult to manage.
She seeks supervised practical training and plans around her children's changing **school needs**.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries her most because robots may arrive around 2031 before she builds a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **field training** and a clear roster plan would help her prepare without promising permanent work.
